text_run.content: In Milvus, segments serve as the fundamental units for data organization. This article offers a comprehensive overview of segments, including their lifecycle and management processes. Understanding these processes allows you to optimize Milvus for improved query performance and system stability.

The data allocated to a shard is transmitted through the same channel<sup>2</sup>, and each shard corresponds to a growing segment. Once the proxy divides the data into shards and sends them to the message queue (Pulsar/Kafka),

the data nodes receive them asynchronously. Milvus maintains a cache for each growing segment on the data nodes, temporarily storing the received data before it permanently persists in storage (S3/MinIO).

A channel is a message queue topic that transmits data to the data nodes in Milvus. Multiple shards can share the same channel, but data from the same shard is always transmitted through the same channel. You can set the number of available channels by changing the
Once the data cached in a growing segment buffer exceeds the upper threshold<sup>1</sup> or times out<sup>2</sup>, the data node writes the data to storage (S3/MinIO) as a chunk.
A chunk is a small part of a segment where Milvus keeps each field's data as a separate file, resulting in multiple chunk files for a single segment.
When the size of the chunks in a growing segment exceeds the upper threshold<sup>3</sup>, Milvus seals the segment, making it a sealed segment that does not permit any new chunks.

Data persistence in Milvus is automatic and transparent to users. However, you can manually flush the data into storage to seal the growing segments, regardless of whether their size reaches the upper threshold. Frequent data flushing creates numerous sealed segments containing a small amount of data, affecting query performance.

As insert operations continue, the number of sealed segments increases. Massive small segments (e.g., less than 100MB) increase data management overhead and slow searches and queries. To address this, Milvus automatically merges smaller sealed segments into larger ones<sup>1</sup>.
In common cases, the data nodes automatically inspect sealed segments in storage and merge smaller segments into larger ones.

When the number of deleted entities in a segment reaches the upper limit<sup>2</sup>, the data nodes also automatically perform compaction to remove the deleted entities from the segment, helping reclaim storage space and improving query efficiency. This indicates that data deletion is an asynchronous operation, and you might see the deleted entities in search and query results shortly after data deletion.
You can also manually trigger compaction if the target collection has a clustering key
<sup>3</sup> so that the data nodes reorganize data in segments based on the clustering key to optimize query performance.

the query node loads the indexes of all indexed sealed segments along with the data of all growing segments and non-indexed sealed segments and subscribes to all shards to maintain a growing segment for each shard

To maintain a growing segment, the query node combines the chunks of a growing segment already loaded and the streaming data subscribed from the message queue to create the growing segment in its own memory.

The subscription to the message queue is asynchronous, so the growing segment in the query node's memory may lag behind that in the data node's memory. You can use different consistency levels to control data visibility in queries. Additionally, the query node creates in-memory temporary indexes<sup>1</sup> for all growing segments and non-indexed sealed segments to support upcoming queries.
When a non-indexed sealed segment becomes indexed, the query node loads its index and clears its temporary index and raw data from the memory
. When compaction happens, the query node keeps the legacy indexes in memory until the index node builds the index for the newly merged segments.

Clustering Compaction is a feature in Milvus that redistributes entities among segments in a collection based on the values in a scalar field called clustering key. You are advised to set an appropriate clustering key based on the filtering conditions in your common query practices to improve compaction efficiency and optimize query performance.
